claims.overstatement: No causal overstatement: the claim keeps 'more likely', and the authors themselves speak of a possibly causal association. Minor points: (1) the 15 (11.3-19.8) and 20.4 (10.2-40.7) compare people who had used cannabis with people who had not (whatever their alcohol or tobacco use; stratifying by alcohol/tobacco was not needed, p. 923), whereas the 4.6 and 7.6 compare with people who had used none of alcohol, tobacco or cannabis; the statement leaves this implicit, and the magnitude's 'cannabis vs none' should read 'cannabis vs no cannabis'. (2) 'the 73% who started in the same year as their first offer': the paper says at the same age, ages being recorded in whole years (p. 923); 'at the same age' is exact. (3) The exclusion behind 20.4 also removed people who used cocaine at once under peer pressure, as the authors note (p. 924), so it is not purely a control for drug-seeking.
claims.note: All numbers checked on rendered pages: four surveys 1991-1994 and 44,624 people aged 12-25 (p. 919; 15,546 + 14,766 + 12,338 + 1,974 = 44,624); 1.9 (1.7-2.1), 4.6 (3.8-5.6), 7.6 (6.9-8.4) (p. 923); 15 (11.3-19.8); about 50% within 2 years vs under 10% many years later (p. 923, Figure 2B on p. 922); 73% and 20.4 (10.2-40.7) (p. 923). Each interval is symmetric on the log scale around its estimate (geometric midpoints 1.89, 4.61, 7.61, 14.96, 20.37). Adjustment: person-years stratified by census tract or block group and survey year (p. 920); covariates sex, race/ethnicity and age group at interview (p. 919), plus age at first cannabis use in the cocaine models (p. 920). Crude context (Table 2, p. 921): lifetime cocaine use 28.6% (3,470/12,114) among people who had used cannabis vs 0.4% (129/32,510), crude OR 100.8 (recomputed 100.8). The relative risks come from discrete-time survival regression. The household frame excludes people with no fixed address, institutions and the military; response 79.2-85.3% (p. 919); ages are retrospective self-reports.

anchors.extracted: NHSDA 1991, 1992, 1993 and 1994a (subsample asked the old opportunity questions); cross-sectional household surveys excluding people with no fixed address, institutionalized people and the military; response 84.2%, 82.5%, 79.2%, 85.3%. Cocaine analyses: 44,624 people aged 12-25 (15,546; 14,766; 12,338; 1,974); cannabis analyses: 26,015 aged 12-18.

Self-reported ages of first chance to try and first use of cannabis and cocaine; no question on first opportunity for alcohol or tobacco; covariates sex, race/ethnicity, survey year, age group at interview; all ages whole years, so same-age events are ties and person-years are kept only up to a tie.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods, end of 7th paragraph (begins p. 919), 8th and 9th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Cocaine models add age at first cannabis use as a covariate; person-years post-stratified by census tract or block group of residence and survey year to constrain neighbourhood confounding (availability, policing, disorganization); supplementary analyses exclude rapid transitions (first use less than 1 year after first opportunity) to constrain drug-seeking.

anchors.locator: Results > From marijuana use to cocaine exposure opportunity, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Against people who had used none of alcohol, tobacco or cannabis, relative risk of a first chance to try cocaine: alcohol or tobacco only 1.9 (1.7-2.1); cannabis only 4.6 (3.8-5.6); cannabis and alcohol or tobacco 7.6 (6.9-8.4).

anchors.locator: Results > From marijuana use to cocaine exposure opportunity, 2nd paragraph (continues on pp. 921 and 923); Figure 2A on p. 922
anchors.extracted: Estimated chance of a cocaine opportunity by 25: 13% with no alcohol, tobacco or cannabis; 26% alcohol/tobacco only; 51% cannabis only; 75% cannabis plus alcohol/tobacco; median age at first cocaine opportunity 17 vs 23 years for cannabis users with vs without alcohol/tobacco.

anchors.locator: Results > From marijuana use to cocaine use, given a cocaine exposure opportunity, 1st paragraph; Figure 2B on p. 922
anchors.extracted: No heterogeneity by alcohol/tobacco history (chi-square 1.77, p > 0.18); about 50% of people who had used cannabis started cocaine within 2 years of their first opportunity; people with no cannabis history quite small at 2 years and under 10% many years later; relative risk 15 (11.3-19.8), cannabis vs no cannabis history.

anchors.locator: Results > Do these observed findings depend on seeking out cocaine exposure opportunities?, 1st paragraph; Figure 2C on p. 922
anchors.extracted: 73% of people who used cocaine started at the same age as their first opportunity; with these excluded, adjusted relative risk 20.4 (10.2-40.7) for people who had used cannabis.
Lifetime cocaine use 3,470 of 12,114 (28.6%) who had used cannabis vs 129 of 32,510 (0.4%) who had not; crude OR 100.8 (84.4-120.3).

Authors describe a possibly causal association and evidence for two mechanisms (more opportunities, then more use once offered) not explained solely by drug-seeking; limitations: cross-sectional data reorganized into sequences, most heavily involved people outside the household frame, retrospective self-report.

Excluding rapid transitions also removed young people whose first cocaine opportunity was unbidden and who used at once under peer pressure, so the supplementary estimates also constrain peer and social influence.

key_findings.note: Fig. 1A at 300 dpi: the alcohol/tobacco curve ends at about 70% at 18 and the other at about 25-26% (read off the figure), as the card says.
Fig. 1B readings (about 88% at 5 years, near 100% by about 13 years) agree with my 150 dpi view; values read off the figure.
The paper says only that the survival regressions gave similar findings; that the estimates are adjusted follows from the Methods (stratified risk sets with covariates), not from this sentence.
Fig. 2B reading agrees with mine (about 40% at t = 0, about 49% at 1 year, about 55% at 2 years, levelling near 75%; read off the figure); the text's 'within 2 years' matches about 50%.
Recomputed from the printed counts: 63.8 (51.2-79.5) and 100.8 (84.4-120.3), crude and unweighted.

reporting_issues.note: About 70% read off Fig. 1A at 300 dpi, below the 75% tick.

Recomputed: race rows total 44,660 and 41,061 (no cocaine use) against 44,624 and 41,025 elsewhere; the cocaine-use column sums correctly to 3,599, and each race row's percentage matches its own counts.
Supported by the crude odds ratios in Tables 1-2, which are reproduced exactly from unweighted counts.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high from confounding: neighbourhood is conditioned on but no individual propensity was measured.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the Discussion's talk of mechanisms and of a possibly causal association goes a step beyond associations located at two points of the sequence, but the abstract is hedged (the associations did not seem to arise solely from drug-seeking).

missed: The card's analysis field gives 'starting cocaine once offered, marijuana against none, 15 (11.3 to 19.8)'; the comparison group is people with no history of marijuana use whatever their alcohol or tobacco use (p. 923), not people who had used none of the three, so 'against no marijuana' is exact. The same wording is in the claim's magnitude.
